claim: Septin proteins evolved from ancestral GTPases.
source: Septin proteins evolved from ancestral GTPases and co-assemble into hetero-oligomers and cytoskeletal filaments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citation to prior work (Leipe et al., 2002) in the introduction.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, five septins comprise two species of hetero-octamers: Cdc11/Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc10–Cdc10–Cdc3–Cdc12–Cdc11/Shs1.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, five septins comprise two species of hetero-octamers, Cdc11/Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc10–Cdc10–Cdc3–Cdc12–Cdc11/Shs1.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by multiple citations in the introduction (Bertin et al., 2008; Farkasovsky et al., 2005; Garcia et al., 2011; Sirajuddin et al., 2007).

claim: Slow GTPase activity by Cdc12 directs the choice of incorporation of Cdc11 vs Shs1.
source: Slow GTPase activity by Cdc12 directs the choice of incorporation of Cdc11 vs Shs1, but many septins, including Cdc3, lack GTPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to prior work (Weems and McMurray, 2017) in the discussion.

claim: Cdc3 lacks GTPase activity.
source: Slow GTPase activity by Cdc12 directs the choice of incorporation of Cdc11 vs Shs1, but many septins, including Cdc3, lack GTPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation (Sirajuddin et al., 2009) in the results.

claim: Guanidine hydrochloride rescues septin function in cdc10 mutants by promoting assembly of non-native Cdc11/Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc3–Cdc12–Cdc11/Shs1 hexamers.
source: We serendipitously discovered that guanidine hydrochloride rescues septin function in cdc10 mutants by promoting assembly of non-native Cdc11/Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc3–Cdc12–Cdc11/Shs1 hexamers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by data presented in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: In S. cerevisiae Cdc3, guanidinium occupies the site of a 'missing' Arg side chain found in other fungal species where the Cdc3 subunit is an active GTPase.
source: We provide evidence that in S. cerevisiae Cdc3 guanidinium occupies the site of a 'missing' Arg side chain found in other fungal species where (i) the Cdc3 subunit is an active GTPase and (ii) Cdc10-less hexamers natively co-exist with octamers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by in silico modeling and phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In fungal species where the Cdc3 subunit is an active GTPase, Cdc10-less hexamers natively co-exist with octamers.
source: We provide evidence that in S. cerevisiae Cdc3 guanidinium occupies the site of a 'missing' Arg side chain found in other fungal species where (i) the Cdc3 subunit is an active GTPase and (ii) Cdc10-less hexamers natively co-exist with octamers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work on other fungal species in the results section.

claim: Guanidinium reactivates a latent septin assembly pathway that was suppressed during fungal evolution in order to restrict assembly to octamers.
source: We propose that guanidinium reactivates a latent septin assembly pathway that was suppressed during fungal evolution in order to restrict assembly to octamers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a proposal based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Homodimerization by a GTPase-active human septin creates hexamers that exclude Cdc10-like central subunits.
source: Since homodimerization by a GTPase-active human septin also creates hexamers that exclude Cdc10-like central subunits, our new mechanistic insights likely apply throughout phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Abbey et al., 2016) in the discussion.

claim: GdnHCl at 3 mM completely rescues the cdc10(D182N) temperature-sensitive proliferation defect at all temperatures tested (up to 37°C).
source: Instead, we found complete rescue by GdnHCl of the cdc10(D182N) TS proliferation defect at all temperatures tested (up to 37°C) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GdnHCl does not have the same rescue effect on cells carrying TS alleles of other septins (cdc3(G365R) and cdc12(G247E)).
source: GdnHCl did not have the same effect on cells carrying TS alleles of other septins, although in its presence a cdc3(G365R) strain grew noticeably worse at 27°C, 30°C and 34°C, and a cdc12(G247E) strain grew slightly worse at 30°C and slightly better at 37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GdnHCl rescue of cdc10(D182N) does not require Hsp104.
source: To our surprise, GdnHCl rescue of cdc10(D182N) did not require Hsp104 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hsp78 is dispensable for GdnHCl rescue of cdc10(D182N) high-temperature growth.
source: Hsp78 was also dispensable for GdnHCl rescue of cdc10(D182N) high-temperature growth (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hsp78 and Hsp104 share the same residues within the ATP binding pocket that contact Gdm in the bacterial Hsp104 homolog ClpB.
source: Hsp78 and Hsp104 share the same residues within the ATP binding pocket that contact Gdm in the bacterial Hsp104 homolog ClpB (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GdnHCl provides partial rescue of 37°C growth by cdc10(D182N) cells at concentrations < 0.1 mM.
source: GdnHCl was sufficient to provide partial rescue of 37°C growth by cdc10(D182N) cells at concentrations < 0.1 mM (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Inhibition of Hsp104 or Hsp78 by GdnHCl in vivo requires concentrations in the medium of ≥1 mM.
source: Inhibition of Hsp104 (i.e., curing of prions) or Hsp78 (i.e., induction of cytoplasmic petites) by GdnHCl in vivo requires concentrations in the medium of ≥1 mM (Tuite et al., 1981)
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GdnHCl suppresses septin defects in cdc10(D182N) mutants via a mechanism that does not involve Hsp104 or its homolog Hsp78.
source: We conclude that GdnHCl suppresses septin defects in cdc10(D182N) mutants via a mechanism that does not involve Hsp104 or its homolog Hsp78.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cells tolerate loss of Cdc10 by assembling filaments via hexameric building blocks in which Cdc3 forms a non-native G homodimer.
source: Cells tolerate loss of Cdc10 by assembling filaments via hexameric building blocks in which Cdc3 forms a non-native G homodimer, but cdc10∆ cells are TS, presumably because at high temperature Cdc3 fails to adopt the homodimerization-competent conformation and/or the non-native Cdc3 homodimer is unstable (McMurray et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: cdc10∆ cells are temperature-sensitive, presumably because at high temperature Cdc3 fails to adopt the homodimerization-competent conformation and/or the non-native Cdc3 homodimer is unstable.
source: Cells tolerate loss of Cdc10 by assembling filaments via hexameric building blocks in which Cdc3 forms a non-native G homodimer, but cdc10∆ cells are TS, presumably because at high temperature Cdc3 fails to adopt the homodimerization-competent conformation and/or the non-native Cdc3 homodimer is unstable (McMurray et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a presumption based on prior work.

claim: GdnHCl fully suppresses the temperature-sensitive phenotype of cdc10∆ cells.
source: GdnHCl also fully suppressed the TS phenotype resulting from a G100E substitution in Cdc10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as well as that of cdc10∆ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At 37°C, GdnHCl-treated cdc10 cells assemble filamentous rings composed of other septins.
source: We confirmed via immunofluorescence with anti-Cdc11 antibodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and electron microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) that at 37°C GdnHCl-treated cdc10 cells assembled filamentous rings composed of other septins.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: In the presence of 3 mM GdnHCl, the fluorescence of Cdc10(D182N)-GFP is restricted to the cytoplasm at temperatures permissive in the absence of GdnHCl for septin ring incorporation.
source: Indeed, even at temperatures permissive in the absence of GdnHCl for septin ring incorporation of Cdc10(D182N)-GFP, in the presence of 3 mM GdnHCl the fluorescence of Cdc10(D182N)-GFP was restricted to the cytoplasm (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: WT Cdc10-GFP continues to localize to the bud neck despite the presence of GdnHCl.
source: WT Cdc10-GFP continued to localize to the bud neck despite the presence of GdnHCl (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In diploid cells co-expressing Cdc10-mCherry and Cdc10(D182N)-GFP, the addition of GdnHCl specifically eliminates Cdc10(D182N) incorporation in septin rings, with no obvious effect on WT Cdc10.
source: Similarly, in diploid cells co-expressing Cdc10-mCherry and Cdc10(D182N)-GFP, the addition of GdnHCl specifically eliminated Cdc10(D182N) incorporation in septin rings, with no obvious effect on WT Cdc10 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GdnHCl is unable to rescue cdc10∆ growth when Cdc3 carries the W364A mutation that blocks Cdc3 homodimerization.
source: As predicted from this model, GdnHCl was unable to rescue cdc10∆ growth when Cdc3 carried a mutation (W364A) previously shown (McMurray et al., 2011) to block Cdc3 homodimerization (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Deletion of DPL1 improves the proliferation of cdc10∆ cells at 30°C.
source: For example, deletion of DPL1, which encodes a dihydrosphingosine phosphate lyase, improves the proliferation of cdc10∆ cells at the moderate temperature of 30°C (Michel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: cdc10∆ dpl1∆ cells are only able to proliferate at 37°C when GdnHCl is present in the growth medium.
source: However, cdc10∆ dpl1∆ cells were only able to proliferate at 37°C when GdnHCl was present in the growth medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In the absence of GdnHCl, Cdc10-less complexes purified from E. coli were detected during high-salt size-exclusion chromatography as a single peak composed of particles containing two or three septins.
source: In the absence of GdnHCl, Cdc10-less complexes were detected during purification via high-salt size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) as a single peak (in addition to a peak of aggregates eluting in the void volume) which, when analyzed by EM, was composed of particles containing two or three septins (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Cdc10-less complexes synthesized in the absence of GdnHCl are unable to polymerize into filaments in low salt.
source: These complexes were unable to polymerize into filaments in low salt (Figure 3D), consistent with our earlier work (McMurray et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In SEC purification of complexes synthesized in the presence of GdnHCl, a new, higher-molecular weight peak appeared containing trimers, tetramers, pentamers and hexamers.
source: By contrast, in SEC purification of complexes synthesized in the presence of GdnHCl a new, higher-molecular weight peak appeared (Figure 3A), which EM analysis revealed to contain trimers, tetramers, pentamers and hexamers (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Cdc10-less complexes synthesized in the presence of GdnHCl robustly polymerize into bundles of laterally-associated filaments upon salt dilution.
source: Upon salt dilution, the Cdc10-less complexes synthesized in the presence of GdnHCl robustly polymerized into bundles of laterally-associated filaments (Figure 3D), very similar to the behavior of WT hetero-octamers that contain Cdc10 (Bertin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fourier transform analysis of the striations in filament bundles formed by Cdc10-less complexes synthesized in the presence of GdnHCl revealed a repeating unit of ~27 nm, the length of a septin hexamer.
source: Fourier transform analysis of the striations in these filament bundles revealed a repeating unit of ~27 nm, the length of a septin hexamer (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Adding GdnHCl to complexes synthesized in its absence does not allow filament formation.
source: Adding GdnHCl to complexes synthesized in its absence did not allow filament formation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GdnHCl likely acts directly on septin proteins, and only when it is present during septin folding/assembly.
source: We conclude from these data that GdnHCl is able to promote septin filament assembly by recombinant Cdc10-less septin complexes produced in a heterologous system that lacks septin-regulatory pathways. Thus GdnHCl likely acts directly on septin proteins, and only when it is present during septin folding/assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Unbiased in silico docking simulations predicted four sites of Gdm binding to Cdc3 with binding free energies of ≤−3 kcal/mol.
source: Four sites had binding free energies of ≤−3 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on in silico docking simulations.

claim: One predicted site of Gdm binding to Cdc3, between the side chains of Thr302 and His262, lies in the G interface and had the second-lowest predicted free energy of binding.
source: One site, between the side chains of Thr302 and His262, lies in the G interface, and had the second-lowest predicted free energy of binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Arg in the position corresponding to ScCdc3 Thr302 is conserved among all Toc34 homologs.
source: Arg in this position is conserved among all Toc34 homologs (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In SEPT2•GppNHp, His158 contacts a highly conserved Asp residue (Asp201) within the Switch II loop of the other protomer.
source: In SEPT2•GppNHp, His158 contacts a highly conserved Asp within the Switch II loop of the other protomer (Figure 4B) (Sirajuddin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and citation to prior work.

claim: In CrSEPT or in human SEPT9•GTPγS, the trans loop 1 His contacts the nucleotide bound by the other protomer.
source: By contrast, in the sole Chlamydomonas reinhardtii septin, CrSEPT, (Pinto et al., 2017) or in human SEPT9•GTPγS, the trans loop 1 His instead contacts the nucleotide bound by the other protomer (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and citation to prior work.

claim: In SEPT2•GppNHp, the Gdm moiety of Arg198 is within ~ 3 Å of the backbone amide carbonyl of His158.
source: The Gdm moeity of SEPT2 Arg198 (residue corresponding to Thr302 in Cdc3) is also within ~ 3 Å of the backbone amide carbonyl of His158 (Figure 4B, Table 1)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Table 1.

claim: The α4 helix was the only region within 5 Å of the trans loop 1 His in every septin crystal structure examined.
source: The α4 helix was the only region to meet this criterion in every structure
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on analysis of crystal structures presented in Table 1.

claim: When Arg was present at the position corresponding to ScCdc3 Thr302 in septin crystal structures, it was always within 5 Å of the trans loop 1 His.
source: when Arg was present at the position corresponding to ScCdc3 Thr302, it was always within 5 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Gdm slightly reduced, but did not eliminate, Cdc10(D182N)-GFP localization to septin rings in cdc3(D210G) cells.
source: Indeed, Gdm slightly reduced, but did not eliminate, Cdc10(D182N)-GFP localization to septin rings in cdc3(D210G) cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Cdc10-mCherry incorporation into septin rings was markedly reduced in cells expressing the Cdc3-AspB chimera compared to cells with WT Cdc3.
source: Consistent with our model, Cdc10-mCherry incorporation was markedly reduced compared to cells with WT Cdc3 (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: S. cerevisiae cells expressing the Cdc3-AspB chimera as the only source of Cdc3 are unable to proliferate at 37°C.
source: S. cerevisiae cells expressing the Cdc3-AspB chimera as the only source of Cdc3 were unable to proliferate at 37°C (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A spontaneous suppressor of the cdc3-aspB temperature-sensitive phenotype was obtained in which proliferation at 37°C was restored.
source: We obtained a suppressor in which proliferation at 37°C was restored (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Sequencing the coding region of Cdc10 in the cdc3-aspB suppressor revealed a single nucleotide change causing the amino acid substitution Q265H.
source: Sequencing the coding region of Cdc10 revealed a single nucleotide change causing the amino acid substitution Q265H (Figure 8D); the Cdc3-AspB chimera was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Incorporation of Cdc10-mCherry into septin rings was partially restored in cdc3-aspB cdc10(Q265H) cells.
source: Indeed, incorporation of Cdc10-mCherry into septin rings was partially restored in cdc3-aspB cdc10(Q265H) cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Gdm was unable to fully rescue the temperature-sensitive phenotype of the cdc3-aspB CDC10+ strain.
source: Finally, Gdm was unable to fully rescue the TS phenotype of the cdc3-aspB CDC10+ strain (Figure 8C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Urea at 0.64 M does not rescue the cdc10(D182N) temperature-sensitive phenotype.
source: We grew WT or cdc10(D182N) cells on solid rich medium containing 0.64 M urea, a concentration we found to slow, but not prevent, growth of WT cells, and saw no cdc10(D182N) rescue (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: A clear zone of rescue was observed around a GdnHCl disk placed on lawns of cdc10(D182N) cells, but not with urea.
source: We saw a clear zone of rescue around the GdnHCl disk, but not with urea (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At 37°C, there was a very slight rescue of cdc10(D182N) by eGdnHCl, and an even less pronounced rescue by aGdnHCl.
source: At 37°C, in addition to the expected partial cdc10(D182N) rescue by GdnHCl, there was a very slight rescue by eGdnHCl, and an even less pronounced rescue by aGdnHCl (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mixing GdnHCl with aGdnHCl or eGdnHCl to a total concentration of 0.75 mM resulted in full or nearly full rescue of cdc10(D182N) 37°C growth, respectively.
source: By contrast, mixing GdnHCl with aGdnHCl or eGdnHCl to a total concentration of 0.75 mM resulted in full or nearly full rescue of cdc10(D182N) 37°C growth, respectively (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 5 mM arginine hydrochloride in the medium provides no rescue to cdc10(D182N) or cdc10(G100E) mutants.
source: Finally, as would be expected if only small molecules like Gdm can fit into the pocket provided by Thr302 and surrounding residues, 5 mM arginine hydrochloride in the medium provided no rescue to cdc10(D182N) or cdc10(G100E) mutants (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The double-mutant cdc10∆ cdc3(T302R) cells are temperature-sensitive.
source: The double-mutant cdc10∆ cdc3(T302R) cells were, like cdc10∆ CDC3+, TS
evidence: This is stated in the results based on data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The addition of GdnHCl fails to restore proliferation at 37°C in cdc10∆ cdc3(T302R) cells.
source: but unlike cdc10∆ CDC3+ the addition of GdnHCl failed to restore proliferation at 37°C (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: When Thr302 in Cdc3 was replaced with Val, rescue by Gdm was observed.
source: By contrast, when we replaced Thr302 with Val – an amino acid with properties similar to Thr, including a short side chain – we saw rescue by Gdm (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The recoded control strain and the P127E D128S K181T T302R Q306D and T302R Q306D mutant strains were indistinguishable from the parental CDC3+ strain in terms of growth at all tested temperatures.
source: The recoded control strain and the P127E D128S K181T T302R Q306D and T302R Q306D mutant strains were indistinguishable from the parental CDC3+ strain in terms of growth at all tested temperatures, and also with regard to the relative amounts of Cdc10-mCherry incorporated into septin rings (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of GdnHCl restored the localization of Shs1-GFP to branch points and hyphal tips in A. gossypii cdc10∆ cells.
source: Addition of GdnHCl restored the localization of Shs1-GFP to branch points and hyphal tips (Figure 5), the same pattern observed in WT cells (Helfer and Gladfelter, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In A. gossypii cdc10∆ cells in the absence of GdnHCl, Shs1-GFP fluorescence was cytoplasmic and diffuse.
source: As reported previously (Helfer and Gladfelter, 2006), in cdc10∆ cells in the absence of GdnHCl Shs1-GFP fluorescence was cytoplasmic and diffuse (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Septin proteins are found in nearly every eukaryotic lineage, with the exception of land plants.
source: Septin proteins are found in nearly every eukaryotic lineage, with the exception of land plants (Auxier et al., 2019; Nishihama et al., 2011; Onishi and Pringle, 2016; Pan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In most extant organisms studied to date, multiple septin proteins co-assemble into linear, rod-shaped hetero-oligomers with at least some potential to polymerize into filaments.
source: In most extant organisms studied to date, multiple septin proteins co-assemble into linear, rod-shaped hetero-oligomers with at least some potential to polymerize into filaments (Fung et al., 2014; Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Oh and Bi, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A number of human diseases and disorders, ranging from cancer to male infertility, have been linked to septin dysregulation or mutation.
source: A number of human diseases and disorders, ranging from cancer to male infertility, have been linked to septin dysregulation or mutation (Dolat et al., 2014; Saarikangas and Barral, 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ability to assemble into quaternary complexes is key to septin function.
source: but within our understanding of septin roles in cellular function one common theme emerges: the ability to assemble into quaternary complexes is key.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from prior work.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of septins reveals septin groups and subgroups that can accurately predict which septin occupies which subunit position within hetero-oligomers.
source: phylogenetic analysis reveals septin groups and subgroups (Pan et al., 2007) that can accurately predict which septin occupies which subunit position within hetero-oligomers (Nakahira et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nearly all septins retain the ability to homo-oligomerize in vitro whether or not they do so in vivo.
source: Moreover, the oligomerization interfaces have not diverged drastically from the ancestral form, as nearly all septins retain the ability to homo-oligomerize in vitro (Farkasovsky et al., 2005; Versele et al., 2004) whether or not they do so in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple septins lost the ability to hydrolyze GTP.
source: Septins clearly evolved from an ancestral GTPase (Leipe et al., 2002) but multiple septins subsequently lost the ability to hydrolyze GTP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In native septin hetero-oligomers most, if not all, of the septin nucleotide-binding pockets are buried within an oligomerization interface, called the G interface.
source: Unlike the building blocks of polymers of the other cytoskeletal NTPases actin and tubulin (and their prokaryotic counterparts), in native septin hetero-oligomers most, if not all, of the septin nucleotide-binding pockets are buried within an oligomerization interface, called the G interface (Sirajuddin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In budding yeast, hetero-octamers polymerize into filaments via the NC septin-septin interface.
source: Particularly for septin complexes in budding yeast, where hetero-octamers polymerize into filaments via the other, so-called 'NC' septin-septin interface (Bertin et al., 2008; Sirajuddin et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most septins retain sequences clearly corresponding to regions/motifs in other small GTPases that contact bound nucleotide and/or change conformation upon GTP hydrolysis.
source: Nonetheless, most septins retain sequences clearly corresponding to regions/motifs in other small GTPases that contact bound nucleotide and/or change conformation upon GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on established knowledge of septin structure.

claim: The baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has been at the forefront of septin research.
source: The baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has been at the forefront of septin research, for a number of reasons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general statement about the field.

claim: The repertoire of septin proteins expressed in yeast (seven) is much simpler than that of humans (13).
source: The repertoire of septin proteins expressed in yeast (seven) is much simpler than that of humans (13).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Two yeast septins are expressed and function specifically during the process of sporulation.
source: Two yeast septins are expressed and function specifically during the process of sporulation (De Virgilio et al., 1996; Fares et al., 1996; Garcia et al., 2016; Heasley and McMurray, 2016; Pablo-Hernando et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Five septins are expressed in nearly stoichiometric amounts in mitotically dividing yeast cells: Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1.
source: leaving five septins expressed in nearly stoichiometric amounts (Kulak et al., 2014) in mitotically dividing cells: Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Yeast septin localization during the mitotic cell division cycle is primarily restricted to the cortex, where septins take the form of filamentous rings at the mother-bud neck.
source: Yeast septin localization during the mitotic cell division cycle is primarily restricted to the cortex, where septins take the form of filamentous rings at the mother-bud neck that undergo a series of discrete structural transitions as the bud emerges and grows and cytokinesis and cell separation take place (Oh and Bi, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Septin filament assembly is essential for yeast proliferation.
source: Septin filament assembly is essential for proliferation (McMurray et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Defects in septin folding and oligomerization translate into clear defects in yeast colony/culture growth.
source: hence defects in septin folding and oligomerization translate into clear defects in yeast colony/culture growth.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical consequence of septin filament assembly being essential.

claim: Two kinds of hetero-octamers co-exist in yeast, with a linear hexameric core of the order Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc10–Cdc10–Cdc3–Cdc12 'capped' at each end with either Cdc11 or Shs1.
